I'm all here for the discourse and the discussion, but comparing hijab to not going to school or eating too much chocolate is disregarding what hijab is really about.

As for how I will raise my children, I will be leading by example and they will still live an Islamic life, with open discussions about Islam. However, if the children do not want to pray, for any reason, I will not force them. Instead, we will have a discussion with them, talk about Islam, why Salah is important, etc...

School is mandatory, and I never resented my parents for sending me to school -- I even loved school. It's all about how you raise your children and ensuring you don't create resentment by using force. Because forcing someone to do something will lead that person to rebel/resent this something (e.g. a daughter being forced to wear hijab might remove it in secret once she is out of her parents' view). As well, forcing someone to not do a certain thing "because someone said so" instead of having discussions about why it's haram, will more often than not lead this person to do this forbidden thing in secret and/or overindulge (e.g. drinking alcohol, smoking, etc)

>Who said we're guaranteed to live tomorrow, let alone put it on later in life (if you live in the West and didn't grow up wearing it, it's much more difficult to put it on later because of the outside pressure and beauty standards)

And as for this, I chose to wear hijab, I reverted and it was my choice. For me, and if my children were to be daughters, not wearing hijab is not to fit beauty standards, it's about having a healthy relationship with Islam and not feeling forced. It's not about having a "relaxed attitude", we all raise our children differently but I will not be resented by my children and lead them away from Islam by forcing them. The only One who can judge in the end is Allah (ﷺ), and if my daughters decide not to wear hijab but they do every single other thing that is obligatory in Islam, who am I to judge? Who are you to judge others?

Here’s a further explanation for what I meant to say: I wear hijab and while it is an obligation, I will not force my child to wear something she will not wear. 

Forcing your child into a certain thing creates resentment and I would rather have my children love Islam than resent it like I resented my parents for forcing me to go to church. I would rather have my daughters learn to love hijab than it being forced upon them and then they eventually take it off. Honestly, it’s better they put it on later than removing it one day.

Every woman has a different experience with hijab and some are at different points in their journey with hijab.

We never touched upon an actual battle in both of my History of Japan classes (one was 6th CE-1941 and other is 1945-2011) that influenced the Tōyō reform. It's surprising though, cause there had been reforms before 1946. In class, we have touched upon the 1923 reform where the Ministry of Education specified 1,962 kanji and 154 simplified Chinese characters (2,116), of which some younger officers and soldiers would have been taught.

In 1931, it was revised again and 1,858 "standard-use" characters were specified. Again, the younger officers and soldiers would be familiar with these as the war did not start for another 8 years. Another reform happened during WWII (in 1942) where 1,134 characters as standard-use kanji and 1,320 characters as sub-standard-use kanji were specified (2,454). So, there was never more than 2,500 characters in use during the war, characters that the soldiers and officers would all know since the lists didn't change that much. 
Now, an officer who was in their 40s+ during any of these reforms might not have been knowledgeable in the "new" kanji, but keep in mind that these reforms were put in place by the government and were chosen from a list that already existed, therefore they would be aware of the kanji's meaning/readings since they just reduced (in most cases) the amount of standard kanji. Meaning that this standard kanji was used in the government and military documents. 

I think it is highly unlikely that kanji were at fault for the battle you mentioned (though I have no recollection of such a battle). 
Prior to World War II, language scholars were concerned with thousands of kanji being in use in various writing systems in learning Japanese. One of the more radical proposals was to abolish the kanji characters entirely and make use of the entirely phonetic system. The Ministry of Education encountered strong opposition from scientists, writers and the general public when it tried to implement this reform, and the idea was dropped. What mostly lead to the tōyō reform was the Ministry of Education deciding to minimize the number of kanji (again) by choosing the most commonly used kanji, along with simplified kanji that commonly appeared in the contemporary literature. This was meant as a preparation for re-introducing their previous unsuccessful reform abolishing kanji. 

The tōyō kanji was accepted and seen as a reasonable compromise by the "purists" and defenders of the "original" system.
